context: Normal subgroup of a group; three equivalent group-theoretic criteria
editorial_screening_reason: ProofWiki lists the equal left/right coset condition, equality under conjugation, and conjugation inclusion as equivalent definitions of a NORMAL SUBGROUP, with N already assumed to be a subgroup of a group G. The one-sided conjugation inclusion for ALL elements g∈G implies equality by also applying the condition to g inverse; omitting 'every g' breaks that equivalence. All three formulations belong under one mathematical meaning, not three separate notions of normality. A normal subset not assumed subgroup would not be the same object, and the normality condition is stronger than ordinary subgroup closure. Nothing assumes a finite group or an abelian ambient group; all subgroups of an abelian group are normal as a theorem. Cosets gN versus Ng depend on handedness and need not coincide for a nonnormal subgroup. All three source formulations describe the SAME normal subgroup, provided normality is tested for all group elements.

context: Quotient group of G by normal subgroup N with coset product
editorial_screening_reason: The source defines G/N only when N is a normal subgroup of G, with left coset product (aN)(bN)=(ab)N. Normality is essential to well-definedness; a quotient SET by an arbitrary equivalence relation, and a coset space for a nonnormal subgroup, need not inherit this group structure. The source's results establish that the coset multiplication is well-defined and the result is a group; do not confuse those theorems with optional defining conditions. The resulting identity is N and the inverse of aN is a⁻¹N, but these conclusions need not be separate definition variants. Left and right coset descriptions coincide as collections because N is normal; no commutativity of the quotient group is assumed. The preexisting quotient-set meaning has distinct weaker structure and is not overwritten. An arbitrary quotient set does not automatically inherit a group multiplication.

formulations.text: Let G be a group and N◁G a normal subgroup. The quotient group G/N is the set of left cosets {gN:g∈G}, with well-defined product (aN)(bN)=(ab)N for a,b∈G.

context: Isomorphism between simple undirected graphs preserving and reflecting adjacency
editorial_screening_reason: ProofWiki's graph-isomorphism entry appears internally inconsistent: its initially stated condition is only one-way edge preservation by a vertex bijection, but it then says 'that is' that both the map and its inverse are graph homomorphisms. These are NOT logically equivalent for general simple graphs. Counterexample: let G have V={1,2,3} and E={{1,2}}, H have the same V and E={{1,2},{2,3}}, and f be the identity bijection. Every G edge maps to an H edge, yet inverse reflection fails for {2,3}, so G and H are NOT isomorphic. The mathematically valid bidirectional adjacency condition is supported by the source's explicit forward-and-inverse formulation, which is also the standard graph-isomorphism criterion. Keep the source's deficient forward-only clause as HELD source evidence rather than approving it. Scope this to simple undirected loopless graphs; multigraph isomorphism would additionally need edge multiplicities. No finiteness or vertex ordering is assumed. The deficient one-way implication is held as source evidence only, not an approved meaning.

formulations.text: Let G=(V_G,E_G) and H=(V_H,E_H) be simple undirected graphs. An isomorphism is a bijection f:V_G→V_H such that for all distinct u,v∈V_G, {u,v}∈E_G if and only if {f(u),f(v)}∈E_H.

context: Convergent ordinary generating function of a real sequence on its real convergence domain
display_term: ordinary generating function of a real sequence
editorial_screening_reason: ProofWiki specifically defines generating function of a real sequence as sum of coefficient times nonnegative integer powers, and defines the resulting function only on z where the power series CONVERGES. The current approved context restricts the variable to real z, a mathematical specialization of the source's undifferentiated z; 0 always lies in D for an ordinary n≥0 power series. Do not silently equate this convergent analytic function with a formal power series in R[[z]], which exists independently of convergence and may have a different target object. Nor is this an exponential generating function involving 1/n!, a moment-generating function, or the double-index generating function the page separately describes. The coefficient extraction notation [z^n]G=a_n is a consequence of the power series presentation, not an extra inequivalent definition; uniqueness of analytic coefficients requires the appropriate analytic interpretation. Convergent real-valued power series is not identified with an unrestricted formal series.
